samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A uses a clean table sorted by due date with fully paid invoices left off. Its status labels are in words ('Overdue 10 days'), amounts are right-aligned with two decimals and the currency is stated in the column headers, and the part-paid invoice shows its total, the amount received and the balance. B is also well ordered, groups invoices into sections and handles the part payment clearly, but its card layout puts dates inline instead of in their own columns, and its amounts don't form a true aligned column the way a table's would. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers leave out paid invoices, sort overdue first and label each one with how many days overdue it is. B puts the amounts in right-aligned numeric columns that line up on the decimal point, shows invoice total, amount received and balance due for the part-paid invoice, and keeps the due date in its own column. A uses cards, so the amounts don't sit in one column and the dates are folded into a text line with the issue date; B is easier to scan at a glance.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers sort the six open invoices from most overdue to least, mark overdue ones with written labels ('Overdue 10 days' / '10 days overdue'), show the $750.00 still owed on #1044, and add up correctly. A edges ahead because it states the currency once in the column headers, gives the $400.00 received its own aligned column, and ends with a totals row. B is just as clear but puts a $ on every amount and mentions the payment only in a subtitle. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pages show only open invoices, put the most overdue first and label status in words (for example "Overdue 10 days"). B edges ahead: it states the currency once in the column headers, gives the part-paid $400.00 its own Received column with a totals row, and its light layout is easier to follow across. A is also strong but shows the amount received only as a sub-note.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages list only the outstanding invoices, sort them most overdue first, label the status in words and show the $750.00 still owed on #1044. B states the currency once in its column headers, shows the invoice total, amount paid and balance in separate right-aligned columns, adds a totals row and puts icons on the status badges. A's choice to put the issue date and invoice total in small text under the customer name makes those figures harder to scan. B leaves the issue date out entirely, which costs it a little on item 5. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages list only unpaid invoices, sorted with the most overdue first, and both show the correct $750.00 balance for the part-paid invoice. A goes further: it has separate Invoice total, Paid and Balance columns with right-aligned figures and the currency stated once in the headers, it adds icons to the status badges, and it ends with a totals row. B tucks the issue dates and totals into the customer subtext instead of giving them their own columns, and its badges rely on text and color only.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both group rows by bench, use word badges (REORDER/OUT) that survive black-and-white printing, show the Oct 3 Thursday-crew line, and right-align the numbers. Neither shows a stock value column or a grand total in the visible area, so both fail that part of item 2. B wins slightly: it repeats the column headings for each bench, adds a legend, and has a Recount column the crew can write in, which makes it more practical on the benches. A's bench bands are clean but its tinted group rows are a bit heavier. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both group rows by bench, show the Oct 3 / Thursday crew source, and mark low stock with REORDER/OUT labels that survive a black-and-white print. Neither visibly has a stock value column, and no grand total shows in the cropped screenshots. A is slightly better: its currency is consistent, its bench headers are clear, and it adds a handy Recount column. B wraps a plant name onto two lines and bolds whole rows, which looks heavier on paper.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B lists all four benches as labelled sections in one compact, plain table. It marks low stock with text and a symbol (▼ Reorder, a boxed ▼ Out) and adds a Recount column, which suits 140 rows. A gives each bench its own page, which is easy to find, and uses solid black REORDER badges. Neither screenshot shows a stock-value column or a grand total, so both score low on item 2, and I scored item 5 as 3 for both because print CSS can't be seen in a screenshot. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A groups rows under clear bench header bands and marks low stock with the text '▼ Reorder' or '▼ Out', which survives a black-and-white printout. It also correctly counts 4 plants at or below reorder level, adds a handy recount column and puts the Oct 3 / Thursday crew source in the header. B looks polished with one page per bench and REORDER labels, but it uses solid black badges, and neither answer shows a stock value column or grand total.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A's layout is plain and printable. It groups rows by bench, puts the source line right under the title, and marks low stock with the words Reorder and Out. B is also well grouped, has clear text badges and adds a useful Recount column. But its dark green header bar and tinted bands are heavy for paper. Neither screenshot shows a stock value column or a grand total, and neither shows its print CSS, so items 2 and 5 are scored on what is visible. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers group the rows by bench and mark low stock with a word (Reorder/Out), so the marking holds up in black and white. B is plainer and prints better: its source line ('Counted Oct 3 by the Thursday crew') is a clear sentence, while A uses a dark filled header bar and tinted rows. Neither shows a stock value column or grand total in the visible area, and neither screenshot shows the print CSS. B's narrow column also makes some plant names wrap.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers compute every row correctly, mark the newsletter swap as n/a with a note, and derive the totals the right way: $4,250.50 spend, 199 orders, $21.36 per order, and 3.58% from 187 of 5,220 clicks. A's footnote says outright that the newsletter swap is left out of the total conversion rate, and its shaded total row stands out a little more. A has the edge on item 5 because its plain light layout drops more cleanly into a monthly deck. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get every figure right: per-row conversion rates and costs per order, totals of $4,250.50 and 199 orders, $21.36 overall cost per order, and 3.6% conversion from 187 of 5,220 clicks with the newsletter swap excluded. B edges ahead because a numbered footnote explains the newsletter swap's n/a cells directly, and its plain light layout should read more cleanly on a deck slide than A's dark card. In both, the footnote marks in the total row (* or a superscript) push those numbers slightly out of line with the column. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get every per-row figure right. Both show the newsletter swap as n/a with a note, and both compute the totals correctly: $4,250.50, 199 orders, $21.36 cost per order, and 3.6% from 187 of 5,220 clicks with the exclusion explained. A's plain light layout is a little better suited to a deck, while B's dark card theme reads less cleanly when projected or printed. Both put footnote markers on the total line, which pushes those cells slightly out of alignment.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover alignment, the mixed revenue, date and churn formats, and the heavy styling, and both give concrete fixes for each column. B ties the column order and default sort more closely to what ops actually does, and its ranked list is tighter. Neither answer clearly says what the table already does well, though B comes closer by noting that n/a is fine for Dune Roofing. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover alignment, inconsistent formats, heavy styling and the sort by ID well. A gives a sharper case for why the column order and sort are wrong, tying them to what ops does and suggesting grouping Plan with Seats and Revenue with Churn. It also offers a small positive note, while B adds extras the request didn't ask for, such as search, filters and churn highlighting. Neither answer clearly says what already works in the table, such as the clear column names.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same main problems: mixed Revenue formats, three date formats, centered numbers, too much border and fill styling, and the ID-first sort. A's worked example table is very concrete, and A says it assumed 'monthly' for the period labels. B ranks its findings more clearly, ends with a top-three quick win, and correctly treats Churn's 'n/a' as text breaking a numeric column, which A calls fine. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the revenue, date, churn, centering, styling and ID-sort problems with concrete fixes. Answer A ranks its findings more clearly, ends with a 'quick win' list of the top three fixes, and treats the text 'n/a' in the Churn column as a problem, which matches the rubric. Answer B has a better column-order rationale, but it says n/a is fine, adds less essential markup and density advice, and its sample table uses an assumed 'monthly' period, though it flags that assumption.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B ranks its findings by how much they likely bother ops and ends with a clear 'three things' summary. It also counts the date formats correctly (three) and suggests an actionable default sort by churn risk or revenue. A covers similar ground but miscounts the date formats as four, calls the seven columns 'five', and doesn't rank its findings. B has a small error of its own: it calls $12,050.5 a 'half-cent' decimal when it's fifty cents. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A ranks its findings, ends with a 'do these three things' summary, and correctly says the dates use three formats. It also treats the n/a in Churn as a problem in a numeric column. B covers similar ground but doesn't rank anything, wrongly counts four date formats, calls n/a fine, and drifts into extras like mobile layout. Neither answer says much about what already works.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend the same 12-row by 6-month table, so both lose points on dimensionality: neither says a flat grid can't hold all three dimensions, and neither offers a gyms-by-classes summary grid for a single period. A edges ahead because it adds a 6-month average column and gives a reason for rejecting the 72-line list. B rejects the list without a reason, though its explanation of why the shading scale should be set per class is slightly sharper. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend the same full 12×6 grid, with gyms nested under classes, and neither uses a gym × class summary as the main view. Both give the same assumption about what the owners will ask and the same fallback. B is better on summaries: it adds a 6-month average column alongside the change column and subtotals. B also gives a real reason for rejecting a 72-line list, while A only says to avoid one.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers lay out a 12-row (class × gym) by 6-month table with a Jan→Jun change column, and both state a clear assumption with a flip-to-group-by-gym fallback. Neither uses the gym-by-class summary grid the rubric expects, and neither explicitly reasons through the three dimensions. A is tighter and notes that averages may not sum meaningfully. B gives a clearer reason for avoiding a list but adds a lot of formatting detail that makes it less of a short decision. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend the same 12-row by 6-month table grouped by class, with gyms nested inside each class. Neither picks a gyms-by-classes grid for one period, and neither says outright that three dimensions won't fit cleanly in one flat grid. B handles totals a little better, including a caveat about whether averages can be summed, while A is more decisive and gives more practical formatting advice, so overall they come out about even.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use the same 12×6 grid with months across the top and a Jan–Jun change column, and neither picks a single summary view such as gyms × classes for the half-year average. A is shorter and gives a clear reason for grouping by class (it puts the gyms side by side), with a fallback if the owners care more about each location. B adds per-gym total rows and useful formatting rules, but its detail on figure styles, minus signs and font size makes it longer than the decision needs. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same core choice: all 72 numbers in a 12-row by 6-month grid with nested groups and a Jan–Jun change column. Neither picks a gyms-by-classes summary view or recognizes that a flat grid struggles with three dimensions. B edges ahead because it states its assumption about the owners' main comparison (gyms side by side within each class), gives a clear fallback, and is tighter, while A spends more space on typography. A does make the per-gym total rows standard, where B leaves them optional.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend a grouped bulleted list, explain why a table would only have filler columns, and say when a table would make sense. A keeps each rule as written, and its headings fit the content better, though it spends a line on bullets versus numbers. B splits the compost rule in two, files the gate code under 'Tools and site', and bolds heavily, so it changes the original wording more than it needs to. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend a grouped bulleted list over a table and explain why: the rules are single sentences, so any extra columns would be filler. A matches item 3 more closely by saying a table would fit once each rule gains the same extra facts, such as consequences or contacts. B places the table only on separate information and adds a short aside weighing numbered against bulleted lists. B keeps the rules' wording closer to the original, while A rephrases and splits some rules, though it keeps their meaning.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend a grouped list, avoid made-up table columns and keep the rules' meaning. B wins on rubric item 3 because it gives concrete cases where a table would fit, such as a rule plus a contact person or a rule plus a consequence. A only describes tables in general terms, and its note that the headings are optional slightly weakens its position. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend a grouped bulleted list and decline to invent table columns. B explains more clearly why a table would leave an empty or forced 'Details' column. It also makes the list easier to scan by bolding lead words and gives a useful note on bullets versus numbers. A is better at naming a concrete case where a table would fit (a rule plus a contact or consequence), but B's opening line covers the same point in general terms, and B's layout is the more polished one.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend a grouped bulleted list, reject the table for the right reason and keep the rules' wording intact. B is slightly better: it names a concrete case where a table would make sense (adding a 'who to contact' column for each area), it is a little tighter, and its gate-code callout tip is practical. A is equally sound, but its closing tips hedge more (it says headings are 'optional' at seven rules). | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend a grouped bulleted list over a table, avoid invented columns and keep the rules' meaning. A is a bit stronger: it names a specific case where a table would make sense (adding a 'who to contact' per area) and suggests a gate-code callout, which is useful. B explains why phones matter well, but it only hints at when a table would fit, and it softens its position by calling the headings optional and offering HTML.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B keeps the table exactly as it renders now, only moving inline styles into the stylesheet, and adds a useful warning that email clients may strip style blocks, though it gives the wrong date (Oct 14 instead of Oct 15). A says plainly that the table was already in good shape, but then makes more changes than needed: bigger padding, a scroll wrapper, a min-width, a heavier header weight and a reworded column header. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A keeps the table looking exactly the same and only moves the inline styles into the stylesheet. It also warns usefully about email clients and the effective date, though it gives today's date as Oct 14 instead of Oct 15. B does say the table already works and why, but then makes four or more changes: more padding, a scroll wrapper with a min-width, a renamed header and heavier header weight, so it drifts toward a rebuild.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say the table already works and keep every price, unit and minimum order. A changes nothing visually: it moves the inline styles into classes and makes a few wording edits, and it sensibly flags the past effective date and the risk that email clients strip <style> blocks. However, it assumes a year in the caption. B makes more changes than a light tidy needs: it adds a scroll wrapper with ARIA attributes and increases row padding, which alters the look of the table. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A and B both rightly call the table good, but both still rewrite it, moving the inline styles into classes and renaming the 'Min. order' header. A also increases the padding and adds a scrolling wrapper, while keeping the prices, units, minimum orders and caption wording unchanged. B renames two headers and rewrites the caption with an assumed year of 2026; it flags that assumption, but it is still invented content, so A is slightly better.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A keeps the table visually almost identical. Its only real changes are moving styles inline, which suits an email to café owners, and clarifying the Min. order header. However, it falsely claims a border change it never made and adds an unneeded date concern. B explains well why the table already works, but makes five changes, including more padding, removing the last row's rule, a scroll wrapper and a CSS rebuild with classes. That goes beyond a light tidy, and B keeps a style block that it admits most email clients will strip. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B keeps the original look almost exactly: same padding, same rules, same alignment. Moving the styles inline is a sensible fix because the list is going out by email, though its 'zebra-free spacing' bullet describes a change that isn't in the code, and its date note invents a problem. A praises the table and then makes five changes anyway, including bigger padding, removing the last row's rule, a scroll wrapper, nowrap and a refactor to CSS classes. It also leaves the email-stripping problem unfixed and only offers to fix it later.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick stacked cards for phones and keep the desktop table for dispatchers. A handles item 4 better: labels stay with the values, the total uses tabular figures, the tracking number is never truncated and gets a Copy button, and its implementation notes are concrete (a separate list using dl, with a warning against restyling the table with display:block). B explains field priority more clearly and puts items last, but its cards drop the field labels. A says the card has four lines while its mockup shows six, and it gives less reason for its field order. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick stacked cards behind a sticky search box and keep the desktop table for dispatchers. B is better on rubric item 4: labels stay with each value (Placed, Total, Tracking), totals use tabular figures with consistent decimals, and the tracking number is never truncated and has a large Copy button. B also gives a sounder implementation route. A explains its field priority a little more clearly, but its date and total line ('Oct 9 · $84.20') has no labels, and B wrongly calls its five-line card 'four lines'.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend stacked cards, lead with order number, status and customer, and keep the desktop table for dispatchers. B handles the small-screen details better: labels stay next to their values, the total is right-aligned in tabular figures, a mockup shows exactly what the rep sees, and it explains why tracking comes first. A puts date, total and ship method on one unlabeled muted line, which is clear enough but weaker on labels. B's claim that both layouts use the same field order is a small inconsistency. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend one stacked card per order and keep the dispatchers' desktop table. A handles item 4 better: every secondary field keeps its label, the total is right-aligned in tabular figures, the tracking number is tap-to-copy and goes first among the details with a stated reason, and status doesn't rely on colour alone. B squeezes date, total and ship method into one unlabeled muted line and puts tracking last, though it does add a useful copy button and carrier link. A does have a small inconsistency: it warns against display:none, then uses CSS to show one layout or the other.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend stacked cards, keep the desktop table, and make tracking tappable and copyable. B explains its field priorities better: order number, customer, status and tracking come first, with date, ship method and total marked secondary, and its layout description has no internal contradictions. A says 'about four lines' but lists five, says every value is tagged though its example omits the 'Total' label, and claims the desktop column order while reordering the fields. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend stacked cards with a pinned search box, keep the desktop table, and put order number, status and customer first. B is better on item 4: it says outright that labels travel with the values, uses tabular figures for the total, and makes tracking both tappable and copyable. A gives the total no label, which is a weakness on that item. B also gives a clearer build route with an accessibility rationale, though it has small inconsistencies: it says 'about four lines' but lists five, and its currency remark contradicts its own '$84.20' example.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B leads with the main causes, mixed decimals and the trailing unit, and orders its fixes by impact: same decimals, unit moved to the header, then tabular figures. It hedges correctly about the font it cannot see. A contradicts itself about Verdana's figures (first proportional, then tabular by default) and puts proportional digits first. It also treats moving the unit to the header as optional and says an in-cell unit is fine. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A correctly identifies mixed decimals and the trailing unit as the main cause. It puts its fixes in order of impact, moves km into the header and hedges about the font, though it oddly lists mixed precision as a 'secondary' problem. B contradicts itself by saying first that Trebuchet MS and Verdana both default to proportional digits and then that Verdana has tabular figures by default. B also leads with the font fix and treats moving the unit to the header as optional, keeping km in its example output.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly explain that right alignment only lines up the end of each string. Answer A presents all three fixes in order of impact and treats moving the unit to the header as a core fix, while Answer B labels it optional. Answer B is also inconsistent: its code formats to 2 decimals, but its final example shows 3. It is a bit more careful than A about whether Trebuchet MS has fixed-width digits. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B covers all three fixes in a sensible order. It firmly moves the unit into the header, while A offers that only as an optional extra. A's advice is internally inconsistent: its code formats to 2 decimals but its example output shows 3. A, however, is more appropriately cautious about whether Trebuchet MS has tabular figures, whereas B claims fairly confidently that both fonts have fixed-width digits.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A covers all four fixes: one fixed number of decimals, with the tradeoff between one and three decimals explained; the unit moved into the heading; and tabular-nums. It also shows the corrected column. B makes moving 'km' into the heading optional, and its annotated diagram gets the decimal-point distances wrong. Both state facts about the fonts' digit widths instead of speaking conditionally. A also wrongly says only some rows end in ' km', when all of them do. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers diagnose the problem correctly and recommend a fixed number of decimals and tabular-nums. B makes moving the unit into the header a core step. It also explains the trade-off between 1 and 3 decimals and right-aligns the header. A treats moving the unit as optional and makes slightly shakier claims about Trebuchet's digit widths. B is longer and incorrectly says the unit appears on only some rows, but overall it is the better fix.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use two sentences and recommend sorting by score from highest to lowest. A's reason ('so the winners lead the page') speaks more directly to what readers want to see, and its only extra advice is a tie-break plus keeping the existing columns. B adds more advice nobody asked for: reordering the columns and adding a rank column. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use two sentences, recommend sorting by score with the highest first, and give a reason aimed at readers, so items 1–3 are equal. Answer A adds column-layout advice nobody asked for (put the score last, add a rank column). Answer B's extra advice, keeping all four columns, is lighter, and its tie-break by grade and then name stays on the question of row order. B's reason, 'winners lead the page', also speaks a little more directly to readers.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers stay within two sentences and recommend sorting by score, highest first. A gives a reason tied to readers (winners at the top) and stays on topic. B's reason ('a science fair is a ranking') is a bit less focused on readers, and it adds advice nobody asked for about column order and alignment. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are two sentences and recommend sorting by score, highest first, with a tie-breaker. B's reason, putting the winners at the top, speaks directly to what readers want to see, and B stays within the question. A's second sentence about column order and right-aligning scores is design advice nobody asked for, and its reason ('a science fair is a ranking') says less about the readers.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer A stays within two sentences, recommends sorting by score from highest to lowest, and gives a reason tied to readers (the winners are at the top). Answer B runs to three sentences, which breaks the length limit. It also adds design advice nobody asked for, like a rank column and a column order, plus an alternative way to group the rows, though its core recommendation is sound. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A has three sentences, which breaks the one-or-two sentence limit, and it adds design advice nobody asked for (a rank column and a column order). Answer B stays within two sentences, recommends sorting by score from highest to lowest, and gives a reason tied to readers: the winners appear at the top. Both answers recommend the right order, but B follows the length and scope rules more closely.
